Paste the new Fountain (or upload the file), run “Screenplay: check a revision” to see what it would do (beats unchanged, reworded, new, gone; lines to record), then “Screenplay: apply a revision”. Applying makes it the story's Fountain, fits the beats already made to it by what they say, numbers the revision and prints it on the script.

fields.label: Story (story entry slug)
fields.helpText: The story this revision is for, e.g. the-devils-shoals.

fields.label: What this revision does
fields.helpText: One line, kept in the revision list: “More narration in Act I; the cabin scene has a longer exchange.”

fields.label: Proposed Fountain
fields.helpText: The whole story as it should be, written in Fountain (edit it anywhere, then paste it here). Use this or File, not both.

fields.label: Fountain file
fields.helpText: The proposed Fountain as a file, for a long script. Use this or Proposed Fountain, not both.

fields.label: How to bring it in
fields.helpText: edit: fit it to what is made already by what it says (unchanged beats keep their picture and recording, new ones are numbered after the beat before). replace: start the story afresh from this text: everything made from the old text goes to the Trash (it can be restored), the new beats are numbered from 1001, and Characters, scenes, masters and voices stay. Use replace for a rewrite where little is unchanged.

fields.label: Status
fields.helpText: draft until it is applied; discarded when you decide not to use it.

fields.label: Revision number
fields.helpText: Set when it is applied.

fields.label: The text it replaced
fields.helpText: Kept when the revision is applied, so you can go back: copy it into a new revision's Proposed Fountain and apply that.

fields.label: What it would do
fields.helpText: Written by “Screenplay: check a revision”: how many beats are unchanged, reworded, new (with their numbers) and gone, and what needs recording or a picture.

fields.label: Beats reworded
fields.helpText: They keep their number, picture and recording; a reworded line is flagged.

fields.label: New beats (their numbers)
fields.helpText: A new beat is numbered after the beat before it (1002a), so nothing after it is renumbered.

fields.label: Compared with (digest)
fields.helpText: A fingerprint of the story's Fountain this was checked against. Applying is refused if the story's text has changed since.

blueprints.name: Shot direction (on beats)
blueprints.description: Adds Shot direction to beats: the shot words a screenplay writes in capitals on a line of their own (ON WILL AND SANDRA, UNDER THE TABLE, VARIOUS SHOTS), which the still reads. For a workspace whose Beat type came with an earlier version; fields a beat already has are left alone.

fields.label: Shot direction
fields.helpText: Where the camera looks in this picture. A Pic note on its own line above the picture in the Fountain fills it on import ([[Pic: Close on the coin in her fist.]]), on a new beat or one where it is empty; or write the shot words yourself (ON WILL AND SANDRA, UNDER THE TABLE, VARIOUS SHOTS). The still reads it; a person or Claude can edit it.

blueprints.name: Screenplay: make a Transcript entry when a transcribe job is done
blueprints.description: When a transcribe job finishes, a draft Transcript entry is made from it: the transcript files, the recording, the language and the length. The job stays the request; the entry is what you open and use. Once per job.

payload.name: Screenplay: make a Transcript entry when a transcribe job is done

blueprints.name: Open call
blueprints.description: Scout talent for the troupe before any story is cast: find or make the actors of a world, take their headshots and fill in their sheets, bring in the voices and give each actor one.

payload.title: Open call
payload.description: Scout talent for the troupe before any story is cast: find or make the actors of a world, take their headshots and fill in their sheets, bring in the voices and give each actor one. A story's casting (who plays which role) happens in the Casting call, from this troupe.

steps.title: World
steps.help: The world whose troupe this is. Pick one or make a new one.

steps.title: The troupe
steps.help: Scouting: the actors of this world, the people who play its characters in every story. Add one with a few words, or upload a headshot of someone and fill in the rest later. Click an actor to open their sheet.
steps.subtitle: build
steps.empty: No actors in this world yet. Add one or upload a headshot.

steps.title: Work on an actor
steps.subtitle: build
steps.help: Pick an actor to take their headshot and fill in their sheet. Skip this to go straight to the voices.

steps.title: Actor sheet and picture
steps.help: The general view is the actor's sheet picture, full figure, in the world's style: upload one here, or fill in the rest of the sheet and make it with AI on the next step (which takes a picture uploaded here as the reference for the person, and replaces it only when you keep the new one). Age views (young, mid, old) are attached on the sheet and tagged age-young, age-mid, age-old; a character's master is made from the view at its age. The rest of the sheet is what stays the same in every role: the base figure, build, hair, skin, the look, the marks that identify them, and what they wear when nothing says otherwise. An animal (Base dog, say) has no hair, skin tone or wardrobe: its coat goes in Look and its markings in Distinguishing features. Set the status to approved once the sheet is right.

steps.title: Make the sheet with AI (optional)
steps.help: Draws the actor's sheet picture from the fields on the step before, on the world's base sheet for their Base (the asset <world>-base-<base>, e.g. storyworld-base-woman or storyworld-base-dog). When the actor already has a picture (its General view, else its first view at an age), that picture is attached as the reference for this person and nothing is replaced until you choose Keep; when it has none, the sheet is drawn from the written fields alone. Fix before making the sheet: a person needs Age, Hair, Skin tone and Baseline wardrobe (the notice above the button says which are empty; an animal needs none of the last three). A person is drawn in four full-length views in one landscape row in their baseline wardrobe; an animal (Base dog, cat, horse or bird) in three views in a row (front, side, back) with no clothes or collar, its coat from Look and its markings from Distinguishing features. A card in Approvals shows the exact prompt and asks before it spends image credit; when the base sheet is not in the Assets library yet it says so and spends nothing. Keep attaches the sheet and approves it; Redo starts a fresh one here at once (it asks before spending again); a skipped or denied one leaves the actor as it was.

paid.cost: Uses image credit. It asks you here, with the prompt, before anything is spent.

steps.title: Voice library
steps.subtitle: category
steps.empty: No voices yet. Upload a clip, record one, or import the workspace's ElevenLabs voices.
steps.help: The voices the troupe can speak with: hear each one, add one from an mp3 or a recording, or bring in the voices on the workspace's ElevenLabs key. The next step gives each actor theirs.

steps.title: Voice casting
steps.help: Give each actor their default voice from the library. A character may name another voice for one story.

checks.label: The troupe has at least one actor
Fix before making the sheet: no person actor is missing Age
Fix before making the sheet: no person actor is missing Hair
Fix before making the sheet: no person actor is missing Skin tone
Fix before making the sheet: no person actor is missing Baseline wardrobe

next.text: Age views: on an actor's sheet, attach pictures of them young, mid and old, tagged age-young, age-mid and age-old. A character's master picture is made from the view at its age.
Now cast a story: the Casting call guided setup lists its roles, shortlists actors from this troupe for each, and makes the master pictures.
Approvals for anything that spends (sheets, masters, takes) show under Automation → Approvals.

blueprints.name: Casting call
blueprints.description: Cast a story: list its roles, look through the troupe, shortlist actors for a role and choose one, give the role to the actor, and make its master picture.

payload.title: Casting call
payload.description: Cast a story: list its roles, look through the troupe, shortlist actors for a role and choose one, give the role to the actor, and make its master picture. The troupe is scouted in the Open call guided setup.

next.text: Cast the next role: go back to Cast a role and pick it. A story that shows one person at two ages has two roles with the same actor.
Give every speaker a voice, then record the lines.
Make the stills with “Screenplay: take a still for a beat”: they take each role's approved master. Approvals for anything that spends show under Automation → Approvals.

steps.title: World
steps.help: The world whose troupe will play this story. Its actors come from the Open call guided setup.

steps.title: Story
steps.help: The story to cast. A story is made in Narrate a story, with its script and beats.
steps.subtitle: status

steps.title: The roles
steps.help: Who the story needs: the characters the Fountain import made, one for each speaker, with the name, age and look the screenplay gave them (in the Role). Add a role the screenplay does not name, delete one it does not need, and set whether we see them or only hear them (a narrator is voice only). The actors come next, one role at a time.

steps.title: Cast a role
steps.help: Pick the role to cast now. Come back here for the next one when it is done: the steps after this are for this role.
steps.subtitle: role

steps.title: Look through the troupe
steps.help: The actors of this world. Look for who fits the role: age, build, presence and look. An actor already cast in this story is marked with the role. This is only for looking: you shortlist in the next step. An actor can play a different role in every story. To add an actor that is not in the troupe, use the Open call guided setup.
steps.subtitle: build
steps.empty: The troupe has no actors yet. A new actor is made in the Open call guided setup, not here.

see_also.label: Add an actor to the troupe
see_also.text: New actors join the troupe in Open call, with their sheet, picture and voice.

steps.title: The shortlist
steps.help: The actors you are considering for this role. Add one with a word on why they fit, and a screen test (the actor dressed as the character) if you have one. On a card, Choose gives the role to this actor and Pass turns them down; you can change your mind. “Add with a screen test” needs a picture; “Add to the shortlist” does not.
steps.subtitle: actor

file.label: Screen test (optional)
file.help: The actor dressed as the character, if you have one. Add a picture and use “Add with a screen test”; without one, use “Add to the shortlist”.

name.placeholder: Leave empty to name it after the role

steps.empty: Nobody considered yet. Pick an actor below.

empty_next.text: Not in the troupe? Add an actor: Open call

steps.title: Give the role to the actor
steps.help: Put the chosen actor on the role, with the age they play and the costume and props for this story. The master picture is made from these, so be concrete: hair, each piece of clothing, what is held or near. Voice (its own section): leave it empty to take the actor's voice, which is filled in a moment after the actor is saved; choose one here for a role with no actor (a narrator), and empty it after changing the actor to take the new actor's.

steps.title: Voice for the lines
steps.help: The role's voice comes from the actor, or one you chose in Give the role to the actor. This gives it to every line the role speaks in this story, so the next take of each line starts with it. It also happens by itself whenever the role's voice changes, but then it only moves lines that have no voice or still have the old one; this button sets all of them, including a line you gave another voice on purpose.
steps.button: Give the voice to the lines

steps.title: Write the master prompt (optional)
steps.help: The master is the approved picture of this character: the actor as this role, at this age, in this costume and props, in the world's style. Every still of the role takes it. To make it here, an AI first writes the picture prompt from everything known about the role (the actor's whole sheet, the character's costume, props and rules, the story and the world's style). It costs a few cents of AI credit and takes a moment; it then shows here and on the next step, where you read and change it before any image credit is spent. To use a picture you made elsewhere, skip this and the last step. The box of what will be sent shows the role's costume, props and rules as they are now, to read only: to change the costume or props, go back to “Give the role to the actor”.

paid.cost: A few cents of AI credit. The actor's sheet, the story and the world's style go too.

steps.title: The master prompt
steps.help: Written by the AI from the actor's sheet, the costume, the story and the world's style; edit it, then make the picture on the next step. It is exactly what is sent to the image model with the actor's picture: change a detail of the costume, the pose or what to avoid, or empty it and write it again.

steps.title: The master picture
steps.help: Leave this empty to make the picture on the next step from the prompt above; upload a picture here only if you already have a master (for example one made from a prompt written with the Storyworld characters skill: it replaces the role's master).

steps.title: Make the master picture from the prompt (optional)
steps.help: Makes the picture from the master prompt (two steps before), with the actor's picture for the role's age as the reference (a picture tagged age-young, age-mid or age-old; the actor's sheet when none is tagged). A card in Approvals shows the exact prompt and asks before it spends image credit; Keep approves the master; Redo starts a fresh one here at once (it asks before spending again). Skip this step when you uploaded the picture. Set the Age on “Give the role to the actor” first: the picture of the actor at that age is the reference.

paid.cost: Uses image credit. It asks you here, with the prompt, before anything is spent.

steps.title: Approve the master
steps.help: Look at the master on the role. When it is right, set the status to approved: the stills take only an approved master. (Keep on a master made here has already done this.)

steps.title: Check the casting

checks.label: Every role we see has an actor
Every role we see has a master picture
Every role we see has an approved master picture

steps.help: Each line is one thing the stills need. A tick means it is there; a circle links to the step that makes it, and to cast another role pick it again in Cast a role.

blueprints.name: Takes of a line
blueprints.description: Pick a story and one of its lines, then hear its takes, add your own by recording or uploading, or have ElevenLabs make one.

payload.title: Takes of a line
payload.description: Pick a story and one of its lines, then hear its takes, add your own by recording or uploading, or have ElevenLabs make one. The take in use is what the story plays.

steps.title: Story
steps.help: The story the line is in.
steps.subtitle: status

steps.title: Character
steps.help: Optional. Choose one character to see just their lines, one after another: the narrator, say, to record all of it in one sitting. Skip this to choose by chapter and beat instead.
steps.subtitle: role
steps.empty: This story has no characters yet. Bringing its Fountain in makes one for each speaker, with their lines.

empty_next.text: Bring the Fountain in: Narrate a story

steps.title: Chapter (optional)
steps.help: A long story is cut into chapters. Pick one to see only its beats, or skip for a short story. (Skipped when you chose a character: their lines are then listed together, whichever chapter or beat they are in.)
steps.empty: No chapters for this story yet. They are made when its Fountain is brought in.

empty_next.text: Bring the Fountain in: Narrate a story

steps.title: Beat (optional)
steps.help: A beat is one shot: its picture and its lines. Pick one to see only its lines, or skip. (Skipped when you chose a character.)
steps.subtitle: picture
steps.empty: No beats here yet. A story's beats are made when its Fountain is brought in.

empty_next.text: Bring the Fountain in: Narrate a story

steps.title: Line
steps.help: The speech line to take. With a character chosen this lists all of their lines in the story, in order, each with its status; otherwise narrow the list with the chapter and beat above, or search it. Each line shows its speaker and first words, then the whole line below it and, when a take is attached, a small "audio" label.
subtitle: text
status
steps.empty: No lines here yet. A beat can be a picture with no words: choose another beat or character, or add a line to this one.

empty_next.text: Add a line: Lines of a beat

steps.title: Takes

buttons.label: Save my recording as a take

paid.cost: Uses speech credit, by the length of the words. It asks you here before anything is spent.

steps.empty: No takes yet. Record or upload one below, or have ElevenLabs make one from the words above.
steps.help: The line is above. Below, add a take: it starts from the line's words, direction and voice, and you can change any of them to try something different (that is what a take is for). Record or upload your own, or have ElevenLabs make it; what needs approving appears right here. Every take stays attached to the line; the one marked In use is the one the story plays.
steps.added: Saved as a take of this line. The take in use stays as it is: listen to your takes, then press Use this one on the one you like best. A take ElevenLabs makes waits for your approval here, then Keep or Redo. Add as many as you like.

working.queued: Being made: anything it asks appears at the top of this step.
working.redo: Making it again: the new one starts within two minutes, then asks you at the top of this step.

paid.cost: Uses speech credit, by the length of the words. It asks you here before anything is spent.

see_also.label: Reorder or add lines of this beat

blueprints.name: Narrate a story
blueprints.description: From a world to a story with its script and cast: the setup steps before the pictures and the voices.

payload.title: Narrate a story
payload.description: Pick or make a world, then a story, bring in its Fountain (write it, or upload the file): the import makes the chapters, beats, spoken lines, characters, scenes and the sounds to fill in. Then check what it made.

steps.title: World
steps.help: The world this story belongs to. Pick one or make a new one. Its troupe (the actors) is built with the Open call guided setup; by the time a story is narrated the troupe should be together.

steps.title: Series (optional)
steps.help: A series the story is an episode of. Skip it for a standalone story.

steps.title: Story
steps.help: The story itself. A new one starts inside the world and series you chose: give it a name here, its premise and setting come on the next step.
steps.subtitle: status

steps.title: Story details
steps.help: The language and the silence between scenes are used when the audio is made. The Fountain is the story itself: write or paste it here, or, for a long script, choose or upload the file under it (one or the other: while one holds the script the other is closed; skip both when the story already has it). Set these now: once the AI is cutting the script, leave the story alone until you have answered its card. Chapters to bring in (empty for all of them, or 3, 2-4, 1,3,5) says which chapters the preview and the import work on.

steps.title: Check the Fountain
steps.help: Reads the Fountain for slips the import would read differently from what you meant, before anything is made: a speaker written in lower case (read as action), a note or a bracket left open, a scene number used for two places, a transition without its colon, a Hold or Sound time that is not a number, invisible characters, a speaker spelled two ways. No AI and no cost; it takes a few seconds. The report shows here under the button when the check is done (it is kept in the story's Fountain check). Its first line says whether the import will stop or go ahead: the import stops only for what is under “Fix before importing”, and goes ahead with what is under “Worth a look” (change one only if it is not what you meant). Nothing needs approving. An uploaded file cannot be edited in Marvin, but it can be read on Story details (Read the file, under it, with the same line numbers as the report): edit it where it came from (on your computer), go back to Story details, choose or upload the file again under Fountain file, then check again. Fountain text written in the story is fixed in the story's Fountain field. Its result is one line that starts “Check:” (the import can go on, or will stop and why); a job that failed says “Failed:” and the reason.

steps.title: Preview the chapters
steps.help: Step 1 of 2 in bringing the story in. A preview only: it works out how the Fountain divides into chapters, beats and spoken lines, with no AI and no cost, and writes it in the story's Split plan. Nothing is made, and its job is named “Preview only: nothing was made”. Chapters start at your `#` section lines; with none, at scene breaks about 12 pages apart. The card above says which chapters it works on: Chapters to bring in, on Story details (or Read the chapters), read when you press the button.

steps.title: Read the chapters
steps.help: The split, as the last preview worked it out. Nothing is imported yet, so you can still change the Fountain: to change the split, go back to the Fountain (the Story details or the upload step), add or move the `#` section lines, and preview again until it is what you want. To bring in only some chapters of a long script, say which here.

steps.title: Make the chapters, beats and lines
steps.help: Step 2 of 2 in bringing the story in. Makes the chapters, beats and spoken lines, and gives each chapter its own part of the Fountain text. It also makes a Character for each speaker, a Scene for each place (and puts the beats in them), and a draft Sound for each sound the words call for, with a score placeholder. Whatever already exists is left alone, so you can bring in a piece at a time and run it again. A long script takes a while (a feature film about a quarter of an hour; you can leave this page). Press the button once: a second press while the import works is skipped, and its job says which job already has the story. Its result is one line that starts “Done: made” and says what it made; a job that failed says “Failed:” and the reason. The card above says which chapters it works on: Chapters to bring in, on Story details (or Read the chapters), read when you press the button.

steps.title: Scenes
steps.help: Where the story happens: one scene for each place the scene headings name (the porch, the galley), made by the import. Check them: a scene brings its place, light and set dressing to its beats, and its ambience (a sound of kind ambience) plays under them, together with the story's own ambience. Add a scene the Fountain does not name with the row at the bottom.

steps.title: Beats and their scenes
steps.help: Every beat of the story with the scene the import put it in, and its chapter (the lists offer only this story's). Change a beat's Scene here to move it, or its hold seconds; add a beat with the row at the bottom. Fix a beat's picture text, sounds and the rest on the beat itself.

steps.title: Sounds: are these read right?
steps.help: What the import read from the words: each sound they name (a splash, a sung song), the bed under each place, and a score. Check only that the sounds are read right (change a kind or a description, or delete one you do not want, the score if there is none). Adding, making and keeping sounds is the Sounds for a story setup.

see_also.label: Make or upload music and ambience
see_also.text: Sound effects too. A link at the top of that setup brings you back to this step.

steps.title: Words that need care
steps.help: Optional. Names and unusual words a voice might get wrong (a ship called the Seagram, a surname): say how each should be spoken. Skip it when nothing needs care.

steps.title: Check what you have

checks.label: Chapters, beats and spoken lines have been made
The characters were made (cast them in the Casting call)

steps.help: Each line is one thing the next stage needs. A tick means it is there; a circle links to the step that makes it. When they all tick, the setup is done: what to do next is listed below.

see_also.label: Cast the roles
see_also.text: Give each character an actor from the troupe and make its picture.

steps.title: Make the script
steps.help: Makes the screenplay from the story's records as they are now: a PDF in Courier 12, the one to share or print, plus the Fountain file, the script as a web page and a breakdown (who speaks and appears, where, which sounds). It is the production script, with the beat numbers, sound cues and directions. No AI and no cost; it takes a few seconds. Nothing makes it by itself: after you change a beat, a line or a scene, press the button again, and the new files replace the old ones (the old ones go to the Trash). It needs the beats: until the import has made them, the button is off and links to the step that makes them. When it is done, open the story (its own page, or Open the story at the end of this setup): the PDF is its Script (PDF) field, under Made by Marvin; the Fountain, the web page and the breakdown are next to it. For the Fountain as it was written, or one with every detail the records hold, run “Screenplay: make the script files of a story” under Automation → Workflows and choose written or complete.

steps.title: Clear what the import made
steps.help: Only if you want to start over: throw an import away and bring the Fountain in again, for example to see how a changed script parses. The button counts what the import made for this story: its chapters, scenes, beats, spoken lines, sounds, characters, takes and castings. Nothing changes yet. The approval (under Automation → Approvals, for an admin) says how many of each, and offers two ways. Move them to the Trash: they can be restored for 30 days. Delete for good: this cannot be undone. Or leave them. Kept either way: the story, its Fountain text and file, its settings, revisions and pronunciations, and every file (pictures and recordings stay in the assets). A sound made for this story goes too, even if another story plays it. Afterwards run Check the split and Bring in the chapters again. Do not run this while an import of this story is still running. The workflow arrives switched off with a package update: an admin switches “Screenplay: clear what the import made” on once under Automation → Workflows.
steps.button: Look at what would be cleared

next.text: Read the story's beats: each is one picture to make. Fix a beat's words or picture on the beat itself.
Cast the actors: the Casting call guided setup starts from the characters this import made and gives each an actor from the troupe, then makes its approved picture.
Give every speaker a voice (Voice entries; import them with “Screenplay: import the ElevenLabs voices”), then record the lines with “Screenplay: record the next lines of a story”.
Make the stills with “Screenplay: take a still for a beat”, cut the audio, then render the video. Approvals for all of these show under Automation → Approvals.

blueprints.name: Sounds for a story
blueprints.description: Start from what the story needs: the sounds its words call for, the bed under each place, the story-wide ambience and the score. Then make what is waiting and keep what you like.

payload.title: Sounds for a story
payload.description: Start from what the story needs, not from a blank form. The import has already listed what the words call for (a splash, a sung song), a bed under each place and a score. Add what is missing and set the beds. Making the sounds waiting is a workflow with one approval for the lot (Automation → Workflows, “Screenplay: make the sounds of a story”). Then place the effects in time on the Timeline.

see_also.text: The sounds a story calls for are read from its script when Narrate a story brings it in.

steps.title: What the story calls for
steps.help: Every sound of the story: an effect is placed at a moment in a beat, ambience is a bed that loops under a place, music runs under the whole story. Each card shows what it is, where it came from and whether it is made. Play a card to hear it; open one to change its words or length. A sound is at most 30 seconds (ElevenLabs' limit): an ambience or music bed with Loop smoothly on is repeated to fill the scene or the story, so make it a steady 20 to 30 seconds with nothing distinctive in it that would be noticed coming round. Add one the import missed below.

steps.added: Added. A sound made now waits for your approval here; one added to the list is made when you press Make this one on its card.

Uses sound-effect credit (music credit for music). It asks you here before anything is spent.

steps.title: Ambience to choose from
steps.help: The story's ambience: a bed that loops under a place (rain on a deck, a quiet cabin). Make one here when a place has none that fits; the next step chooses it under its scenes, and “Ambience and music for the whole story” can run one under every scene. Play a card to hear it. A sound is at most 30 seconds (ElevenLabs' limit) and an ambience is made to loop, so describe a steady 20 to 30 seconds with nothing in it that would be noticed coming round.

file.help: Optional: record or upload a sound, or choose one from your assets, instead of having one made.

paid.cost: Uses sound-effect credit. It asks you here before anything is spent.

# Screenplay Studio

Screenplay Studio is the pipeline, not any one world. A **world** (Storyworld is the first; another could be anything) is just records inside it: a `world` entry, its actors, its stories. This skill covers the pipeline; a world's own skill covers its look and its cast.

**In a Marvin workspace the records are the source of truth.** Read references/marvin.md first: what each record holds, the workflows, and the stages from idea to video. Then references/recent.md for what was added later (v180 on), and references/recent-older.md for v128 to v179 (the readiness check, batch approvals, Fountain checks, the story's ambience bed, recording by character).

- **Writing a Fountain from an idea (or asking an AI to):** read references/fountain.md first. It lists what to decide before writing, the title page (including `Setting:` and `Premise:`), the structure, how to introduce each character, dialogue, pictures, timing, sound and notes, a skeleton, and a check to run before importing. What the file does not say is empty in Marvin.
- **Cutting a Fountain into beats:** the story is one Fountain document (written by you or by an AI) in its Fountain field. The import cuts it with no AI: a `#` section line is a chapter, a scene heading with its first action is a picture, each further action is another, a page break (`===`) always starts a new picture, and each speech is a spoken line. It also makes a Character for each speaker, a Scene for each place and a draft Sound for each sound the words call for. A beat is one picture with its words and sounds, the same as a shot-list row, not a plot beat.
- **One place to edit:** the story's Fountain. Bring it in again after changing it (Refresh adds, updates what nothing has been made from, moves what is gone to the Trash, keeps and flags anything with a picture or recording). The Script job with *version: complete* writes the records back out as a Fountain, and *written* writes the Fountain as it was written. To start over instead, *Clear what the import made* (`screenplay-clear-story`) counts what the import made, then an admin moves it to the Trash or deletes it for good; then import again.
- **Casting:** read references/actors.md. One actor can play the same person at several ages; tag the actor's views `age-young`, `age-mid`, `age-old` and give each Character an Age.
- **Workers:** one container image, `screenplay-studio-worker`, tagged with the package version it goes with; see docker/README.md in the repository. A queued job that nobody picks up usually means no worker offers its kind: check Settings -> Workers.

Rules that cost time:
- Preview first (`import-beats` and `render` accept a preview), and say what was done in your own words, not only what a job logged.
- Anything that spends credit (images, voices) is asked about first; nothing is published without the author's approval.

# Actors, characters and casting

Three records, kept apart. An **actor** belongs to the *world's troupe*: the look that stays the same in every role. A **character** (`cast-member`) is that actor in **one story**: a role, a costume and props. A **casting** is the search for who plays a role: the candidate actor, how well they fit, a screen test, and whether they were chosen or passed. The same actor can play a different character in the next story. A peg leg or a false beard is a costume or prop of the character, not part of the actor. The narrator can be a **voice-only** character with no picture.

## Bases belong to the world

A *base* is the general figure an actor is made from: proportions and silhouette. A world lists its bases in its `bases` field, each with a base sheet picture (`base_sheets`). Add a base only when making an actor from another one would look wrong (a different body, not a different person). Age within a base is the actor's business. An animal is a base of its own (`dog`): its sheet is three views in a row, not four, and its coat goes in `look` and its markings in `distinguishing_features` (hair, skin tone and wardrobe do not apply). *Make an actor's sheet* draws either from the world's base sheet, the asset `<world>-base-<base>` (see recent.md, v182).

## The actor record

Fill the `actor` fields from the actor's picture and the brief. Leave a field empty rather than guess; an age is a proposal until the author confirms it.

| Field | What goes in it |
|---|---|
| `title` | the actor's name (the slug is the name in lower case) |
| `world` | the world's slug |
| `base` | one of the world's bases |
| `presence` | `on screen`, or `voice only` for a voice actor (no picture; use a shared featureless placeholder as the `general_view`) |
| `age` | years, only when set |
| `build`, `hair`, `skin_tone` | one line each. Skin tone describes the artwork, not ethnicity |
| `look` | the general look: the face and manner that stay the same |
| `distinguishing_features` | what picks them out in a lineup (a beard, an earring, a hairstyle). Not costume |
| `baseline_wardrobe` | what they wear in the plain sheet. A role's costume replaces it |
| `general_view` | the actor's sheet picture |
| `age_views` | more pictures of the same person at other ages (see below) |
| `voice`, `voice_sample` | their default voice (a voice record's slug) and a clip to hear it |
| `status` | `draft` until the sheet is approved |
| `notes` | anything else that is established |

Do not put story role, family relationships or personality on the actor from how they look. Only established facts are recorded.

**Name the picture file for the actor** (`Nell.png`, not `image-3.png`): in Marvin, "Create entry from asset" turns the file name into the actor's name and slug.

## A paid sheet (Screenplay: make an actor's sheet)

A person's sheet is one landscape picture (1536x1024): four full-length views of the actor side by side in one row, front, three-quarter, right-side profile and back, soft ground shadows on plain warm cream, no text; an animal's is three views in a row. It is made from the world's base sheet (proportions), `style_actor`'s sheet (the finish only: flat matte shapes, dot eyes, a tiny smile; never that actor's face, hair, skin, clothes or colours) and a picture of this person for the face, hair and build, never its clothes: the `source_picture` input when given (a face crop), else the actor's own `general_view` (an uploaded picture: the new sheet keeps that person and only fixes the layout and finish), else its first `age_views` picture, else none. Before paying for it fill `age`, `build`, `hair`, `skin_tone`, `look` and `baseline_wardrobe` (and `distinguishing_features` if there are any): an empty field is sent as "not specified: choose something plain that differs from the style actor", so the model chooses for you. Open call's *Check the troupe* lists *Fix before making the sheet* lines for a person actor with no Age, Hair, Skin tone or Baseline wardrobe. The picture is shown in the Keep question and becomes the actor's `general_view` only on Keep; a Redo, a skip or a no leaves the actor as it was, its own picture still attached.

## The character record

A character is made from an actor, not from scratch. Fields: `story`, `actor` (the actor's slug), `role`, `speaker` (the one-word name its speech lines use as the cue in the Fountain), `presence`, `age_state` (young, mid, old), `costume`, `props`, `rules` and `master` (the approved picture). Stills attach the approved master, so an unapproved master blocks them.

**`rules`** is what must hold in every picture of this one character (which side a peg leg is on; that the face matches the same person at other ages). The world holds only the style, so a rule about one person lives here; the still and master workflows put each character's costume, props and rules into the prompt.

## The casting record

`story`, `role`, `character`, `actor` (the candidate), `state` (what the role needs at that point), `fit` (why this actor does or does not fit), `status` (`considering`, `auditioned`, `chosen`, `passed`) and a `screen_test` picture. Search the troupe on the hard fields (presence, base, age range) first, then judge look and voice by eye and ear and write the verdict in `fit`. A role that fits nobody is a gap: make a new actor.

The **Casting call** guided setup (Setups) walks it for one story: pick the world and the story, list the roles (the characters), look through the troupe, shortlist actors for a role (each shortlisted actor is a casting record, with a note on the fit and an optional screen test; mark one Chosen and the others Passed), give the role to the chosen actor with the age and the costume and props, then the role's master picture: an AI writes the prompt from everything known about the role (you read and edit it, it is kept on the role as Master prompt), the picture is made from exactly that prompt, or you upload one made elsewhere (made there it starts from the actor's pictures tagged for the role's age, so tag one `age-young`, `age-mid` or `age-old` first; uploaded it is one you made outside, for example from a prompt the Storyworld characters skill wrote), and approve it. Do the next role by picking it again. The Open call scouts the troupe first; Narrate a story brings in the script and beats.

## Reading what is in Marvin

`marvin platform entries get <slug>` returns an actor's or character's fields and its attached pictures with their URLs. Download the picture to attach it as a reference; do not describe it from memory.

## One actor, many ages (views tagged by age)

An actor has **Views at different ages** (`age_views`): as many pictures of the same person as you like, at other ages and angles. In the Assets library tag each one **`age-young`**, **`age-mid`** or **`age-old`**, and `face-closeup` or `profile` where it is one. A Character (`cast-member`) has an **Age** (`age_state`: young, mid, old). The **`screenplay-make-master`** workflow reads the Character's actor, collects up to four of the actor's pictures tagged for that age, and makes the master from them, the costume and props, and the world's style: it asks before spending image credit, then Keep or Redo, and Keep approves the master.

Rules that keep one man one man across 18, 30 and 52: put the features that never change (brow shape, nose, jaw, a scar, the hair parting) in `distinguishing_features` and keep them in every version; make the young and old masters early and approve them as a pair, side by side; a still takes the approved master, not the raw views (the plain actor sheet fights the costume), except a tagged `face-closeup` when a shot is a reuse of a face. A story that shows the same person at two ages has two Characters pointing at the same actor.

## Writing a master prompt

The **master** is one reference portrait of a character: the actor, as this role, at this age, in this costume. Every still takes it, so the prompt has to pin down the person and the costume, and leave the story out. The image model gets the actor's picture(s) with the prompt; the prompt says what to keep from them and what to change.

1. **Open with the references.** Say the attached picture(s) show the same person and that their face, head shape, eyes, brows, nose, jaw, hair colour and build stay exactly as shown, at the age of the role.
2. **The person.** Age, build, hair, skin and the features that must always be kept, from the actor's sheet. Use the sheet's own words (for example a minimal face with small dark ovals for eyes). Do not infer ethnicity, gender or personality from hair or clothes.
3. **The costume.** Every piece, with colour, material and where it sits, from the character's costume. Say which side something is on when it matters (a ring on the left hand, a cutlass on the left: do not mirror).
4. **Props.** Only what the character wears or holds. Furniture, animals, the place and the weather belong to the stills, not the master.
5. **Pose and frame.** One full-body three-quarter portrait, standing relaxed, on a plain neutral background in even soft light, nothing else in the frame.
6. **The world's style.** Carry the world's style rules: soft, matte, hand-painted miniature rendering, never photographic; heads large and rounded; each hand four fingers and a thumb, never added or dropped; no readable text or writing anywhere.
7. **The character's rules** hold in every picture: put them in as they are written.
8. **Length and form.** 120 to 220 words of plain sentences: no heading, no list, no quotation marks. Use only what is known; leave out what is not. Where the costume and the actor's features disagree, keep the actor's features.
9. **The person's extra instructions** (a softer smile, hands visible) are added last and win over the defaults, unless they break a rule above.

**Guardrails the workflows apply themselves (v130).** The prompt writer is told that the extra instructions may change the person only, so a note that names a place, weather or action ("on a storm-tossed deck") has that part left out; and it writes every side-specific thing as the character's own *anatomical* left or right (a model mirrors "left" otherwise). Whatever the prompt says, *Make the master* adds a fixed closing paragraph, shown in the approval: one character alone on a plain neutral background, no scene, weather, furniture, animals or other people, anatomical sides never mirrored, no writing. A still's prompt says that reference pictures other than a character's own (a place, a style sample, a cover) give the place, light and style only, and nobody who appears only in a reference is drawn.

# Writing the Fountain: from an idea to a file the import reads completely

The story is one Fountain document. The import reads it with no AI and makes the chapters, beats, lines, Characters, scenes and sounds from it, so **what is not in the file is empty in Marvin**. This page says what to write so nothing is missing. Follow it when you write a Fountain from an idea, when an AI writes it, and when you ask an AI to edit one.

## 1. Before writing: answer these

If the idea does not say, decide (or ask) before writing a line. Each answer has a place in the file.

| Answer | Where it goes in the file | Becomes in Marvin |
|---|---|---|
| Title, who wrote it, where it comes from | title page: `Title`, `Credit`, `Author`, `Source` | the story's credits, printed on the script |
| One or two sentences: what the story is about | title page: `Premise:` | the story's **Premise** (the picture workflows read it) |
| Where and when it happens, in one sentence | title page: `Setting:` | the story's **Setting** |
| Format and length | title page: `Format:` | kept with the story |
| Who is on screen: name, age, sex, what they are, what they wear and carry, one thing that marks them | the first action line that brings each in | a **Character** (Role holds the sentences) |
| Who only speaks (narrator, announcer) | `NARRATOR (V.O.)` cue | a voice-only Character (no picture) |
| The places | scene headings | a **Scene** per place |
| What the story sounds like | `[[Sound: …]]` notes, weather words, `~` lyrics | **Sounds** to generate or upload, an **ambience** bed per place |
| What each part is about | `= synopsis` line under each scene heading | the chapter's summary, and the setting if none is given |
| How the story is divided | `# ACT …` lines | **chapters** |

The **World** (which look and rules the pictures follow) is not in the file: choose it on the story in Marvin. The import says when it is missing.

## 2. The title page

First lines of the file, `Key: value`, one blank line after. A value that needs several lines continues on lines indented by four spaces.

```
Title: THE DEVIL'S SHOALS
Credit: Written by
Author: Jared
Source: Original story
Draft date: November 2026
Format: Short Screenplay
Setting: A pirate brigantine wrecked on a cursed reef, one stormy night.
Premise: A ruthless captain and her cabin boy survive a wreck and meet the drowned crews of every ship the reef has taken.
Contact:
    Agent: Blackbeard Literary
    info@example.com
Copyright: (c) 2026 Jared. All rights reserved.
```

`Setting` and `Premise` fill the story's fields when they are empty. Without `Setting:` the import uses the first scene's synopsis, else the first place. **It never invents a premise**: with none, the import names it as missing. Keep every title-page line when an AI edits the file: they are lost easily.

## 3. Structure

- `# ACT I: THE WRECK` starts a **chapter** (use `# ACT II …`, `# ACT III …`, or numbered `## 03 The heist`). Without any `#` line the import cuts chapters by length (about 12 pages each, between two scenes), and a short script is one chapter, whose numbers turn clumsy (`00a`, `00b`…). Keep these lines in every revision.
- `## SCENE 2: THE REEF` is a label, kept as written.
- A scene heading starts a place: `INT. CAPTAIN'S CABIN - NIGHT #2#`. **It must start with `INT.`, `EXT.`, `EST.` or `INT./EXT.` (`EXT/INT.`, `I/E.` and `E/I.` work too)** (or a leading dot, `.UNDERWATER - CONTINUOUS`): `UNDERWATER - CONTINUOUS` is not a scene. Spell a place the same way each time: the same place at another hour is one Scene. The `#2#` number is optional and keeps a scene's identity through revisions.
- Under each heading write one synopsis line: `= Captain Valerie refuses to back down despite the cabin boy's pleas.` It becomes the chapter's summary.

## 4. Characters

Introduce each person **once**, in capitals, the first time they appear in the action, with their age and the sentences that say what they look like. The import copies those sentences into the Character's Role, reads the age and the sex (from the pronouns or a word like *boy*, *woman*, *lad* in them) into the Character's **Age** and **Sex** fields, and sets **Age state** (young under 30, mid under 55, old after) from the age, which picks the actor's picture of that age for the master. A Character made before these fields existed gets them on the next import, only where they are empty.

```
CAPTAIN VALERIE "THE VULTURE" VANE (40s) stands over the desk. She wears a rain-soaked tricorn hat and a long leather coat. One eye is clouded over with a cataract. She jams a compass into her belt.

CHET (20s), a young cabin boy, clutches a waterlogged logbook.
```

- Both `NAME (40s)` and `NAME, 40s,` are read. Use the first.
- Say the sex with a pronoun or a word, say what they wear and carry, and give one mark that tells them apart. **A costume the file never mentions is empty**, and the picture falls back to the actor's own clothes.
- A speaker the file never introduces gets a Character with only a name.
- A narrator or announcer is written `NARRATOR (V.O.)`; someone heard but not seen, `CHET (O.S.)`. Neither is in a picture.

## 5. Dialogue

```
CHET
(shouting over the storm)
The hull is groaning, Captain!

VALERIE
(sneers)
Drop anchor in a graveyard, boy?
```

- A cue is **all capitals, alone on its line**. **Never put a capitals line above action text:** the import makes it a speaker, and that person reads the action aloud. A sound is made only from a `[[Sound:]]` note (or `the sound of X`): a word or a line in capitals is never a sound, and a capitals line standing alone is read as action. If a line of capitals must be action, start it with `!` (`!THE PLAGUE OF THE SEA RISES.`).
- A blank line between speakers. No dual dialogue (`^`) unless two voices must overlap: `NAME ^` on the second speaker's cue, after a blank line, plays that line at the same time as the one before (v210).
- The parenthetical is the delivery note (kept with the line).
- A beat holds at most 6 lines; the next starts a new one.

## 6. Pictures, timing and transitions

- Each action paragraph is part of a **picture** (one still). Action right after speech starts a new one. A paragraph is cut after about 420 characters.
- **`===` on its own line always starts a new picture.** Use it when the camera, place or subject changes inside one scene. By default one picture is one moment, not one per sentence; to ask for more pictures, and say what each shows, use `[[Pic:]]` (below).
- A silent picture plays 4 seconds. To change it: `[[Hold: 1.5s.]]` on its own line inside that picture. A picture with speech lasts as long as the take. Put no pause after every line.
- Transitions go on their own line, in capitals, ending in `TO:`: `CUT TO:`, `DISSOLVE TO:`, `CROSSFADE TO:`. Any such line is a transition: one that names a dissolve or a fade is that, every other (`BACK TO:`, `FLASHBACK TO:`, `WIPE TO:`) is a cut with its words kept. A transition belongs to the picture that comes after it. `FADE IN:` before the first picture brings the film up from black; `FADE OUT.` after the last one takes it down to black. A transition never changes how long the film is.
- A transition's length: `[[Transition: 1.2s.]]` inside the picture it leads into (empty: the story's length, else 0.5 s).
- Something that happens at a word: a note among the words of a speech, `The hammer strikes [[Sound: clang | Camera: punch]] the wheel.` or `…in 1977, [[Pic: a small probe in dark space]] had needed…`. The voice and captions never read it; a Sound plays at the end of the word before the note, a Pic is a picture of its own that dissolves in at the word after it (v211); a Camera moves the camera there: `punch` (a quick zoom in and back; `punch 1.1`), `shake` (`shake 2`), `nudge 0.7,0.4` (a drift toward that point) (v212). Also `whip-pan left` or `whip-pan right 0.5` (a fast sweep and back), `sway` or `sway 1.5 3` (a handheld wobble: % of the frame, seconds) (v218). A Look changes the picture there for a moment (v218): `[[Look: flash]]` (`flash orange 0.6 0.4`: colour, brightness, seconds), `burn`, `dip` or `dip white 1.2` (seconds), `freeze 1`, `tint sepia` (mono, cold, warm; `tint cold 0.5 2`), `blur 0.6` (strength; `blur 2s`), `vignette 0.8 2`, `glitch`: after the kind a colour, then the amount, then the seconds, any left out, and `2s` is always seconds. `Nudge: 0.1` beside a Look moves it too. A Mix changes the sound under the voice there (v219): `[[Mix: dead-air 2]]` (the beds, the music and the sounds go silent for 2 s, all but a Sound in the same note), `[[Mix: duck 0.3 2]]` (they dip to 0.3 for 2 s); `[[Emphasis]]` (or `Emphasis: 1.5`) shows the word after it bigger in the captions.
- A line that should start earlier or later than it falls (an interruption): `[[Nudge: -0.4]]` on its own line right before the speaker (or right under the speaker's name). Seconds; a negative nudge overlaps the line before. It fills the line's *Nudge* (v209).
- **A card in the film** (`THREE YEARS LATER`, a chapter's title, `THE END`): centred text in a paragraph of its own, `> THE END <`. It is a beat that shows the words on the story's card colour, with no picture made for it. A second centred line under the first is a sentence under the title. A speech right after it is read over the card. It plays 4 seconds, or as long as its lines; `[[Hold: 2s.]]` changes that. Centred text inside a paragraph of action is still action.
- A title over a picture: `SUPER: THE DEVIL'S SHOALS` as an action line.

### One picture per sentence, or a picture you direct: `[[Pic: ...]]`

`[[Pic: Close on the coin in her fist.]]` on a line of its own starts a new picture, as `===` does, and its words become that beat's **Shot direction**: the field the still's prompt reads as where the camera looks, which a person (or an AI) can read and edit later. `[[Pic]]` or `[[Pic.]]` starts a picture with no direction. Every other Fountain app reads it as a note and ignores it, so the file is still an ordinary screenplay anywhere else.

- Use it in place of `===`, or beside one: a Pic note and a `===` written together are one break. It may sit right above the speaker or the action of its picture, with no blank line; but leave a blank line after a speech, since a Pic note right under a speech's last line is inside the speech, and only a note.
- Right under a scene heading (or above it) it directs the scene's first picture; it never makes a picture of the heading alone. With nothing after it (before `FADE OUT.`, or at the end) it makes no picture.
- Two Pic notes with nothing between them are one picture with the first one's words; the check says the second is ignored. A Pic note inside a speech, or in the middle of a line, is only a note (the check says so too).
- Keep it to the shot: where the camera is and what the frame holds, in a sentence. The check flags one over 400 characters.
- The note stays in the beat's own Fountain text. Rewording only a Pic note is not a revision of the beat; adding or removing one moves where pictures break, as adding or removing `===` does. An import fills Shot direction on a new beat, or on one whose field is empty; one a person wrote is never written over.

A picture for each spoken sentence:

```
[[Pic: Wide on black rocks in a storm, a wave vanishing between them.]]
Black rocks break the surface like teeth.

NARRATOR (V.O.)
There was a channel through the Devil's Shoals.

[[Pic: Medium wide: a lane of dark water between two rock walls.]]
Between two black walls of rock, a lane of dark water opens.

NARRATOR (V.O.)
Wide enough for a ship.
```

Every picture is a still to make (and pay for): count the Pic notes before you bring the story in. The import's preview says how many beats it would make.

### An info card and what stays changed: `[[Info card: …]]`, `[[Changes: …]]`

Two more notes belong to the picture they sit in, wherever in its text (under its Pic note, under its action, after its speech), each on a line of its own and outside a speech. They start and end no picture, and every other Fountain app ignores them as notes.

- `[[Info card: label | title | sentence]]` is the card shown over the picture: the beat's **Info card** label, title and sentence. Any slot may be empty (`[[Info card: | Day one | The fleet is alone.]]`), but one must have words. One slot alone is the **title**: `[[Info card: 2302]]`. Two slots are the label and the title.
- `[[Changes: the lead ship's hull is scorched black.]]` is the beat's **Changes from here on**: what stays changed in every later picture.
- An import fills them on a new beat, or on one whose field is empty; a value a person set is never written over (an info card is one thing: a beat with any of its three set keeps its own). A plain card's centred words are its card, so a note does not change them.
- One with no words, in the middle of a line or inside a speech is only a note: the check says so (worth a look).
- The *complete* script writes both notes back, so it reads back as the same beats.

The card over the first picture of a chapter:

```
# Chapter 4

EXT. INTERSTELLAR SPACE - 2302

[[Info card: CHAPTER 4 | 2302]]
[[Pic: Wide on three generation ships against the stars.]]

NARRATOR (V.O.)
Three ships left the old sun behind.
```

## 7. Sound

- Name each sound yourself: `[[Sound: timber grinding against rock at 0.4s.]]` (seconds into the picture; leave `at` off for the start). Describe the **sound**, not the story: "a single sharp splash", not "Chet falls in". When a picture has `[[Sound:]]` notes, only those are made.
- Without a note, the import reads `the sound of X`, `a X sound` and a loud capitalised word, and keeps the sentence as the prompt.
- Lyrics start with `~`; they become one music Sound.
- Rain, thunder, wind and waves in a place's action make its **ambience** bed. Describe the weather once per place.
- The score is a placeholder made for every story: delete it if there is none.

## 8. Notes

`[[ anything ]]` is removed before pictures, narration and subtitles, so it is safe for comments. Only `Hold:`, `Sound:`, `Pic:`, `Camera:` (among a speech's words), `Info card:`, `Changes:` and `Nudge:` notes are acted on (a Pic note starts a picture; the last two fill the beat's info card and changes: see section 6). A note must have no blank line inside. Do not put story in a note.

### What the *complete* script carries back (v204)

The *complete* script (Make the script, version complete) is made from the records and drops nothing the import was given:

- Your own notes come back where you wrote them: those under the title page (`[[Production: …]]`, `[[Visual style: …]]`, `[[Continuity: …]]`, `[[Timing: …]]`) after the title page, and each note in a picture (`[[Sentence: …]]`, `[[Silent on purpose: …]]`, `[[One picture: …]]`, a comment) in the same picture, above its Pic note, right under it, or after its lines, in the same order. A note inside a speech is the line's and is not carried. The notes the export writes itself (Pic, Beat, Scene, Ambience, Info card, Changes, Hold, Sound) are written from the records, never twice.
- A picture with a `[[Pic:]]` note has no `===` above it: the note starts the picture. A picture without one keeps its `===`.
- It reads back what it wrote: a scene's Place, Light, Set dressing and Continuity from `[[Scene <name>. Place: …. Light: …. Set dressing: …. Continuity: ….]]` (the scene the note names only), and a beat's Focus and Expression from `[[Beat NN. … Focus: …. Expression: ….]]`, both as the export writes them (each part once, in that order; otherwise the check says the note is not read). A new scene or beat takes them; one that exists only into an empty field, never over one a person set.
- Not read back yet: a beat's Camera, Cast and Note, and a scene's ambience level, from those notes; a field that had no final full stop comes back with one.

## 9. A skeleton

```
Title: …
Credit: Written by
Author: …
Source: …
Draft date: …
Format: …
Setting: …
Premise: …

# ACT I: …

## SCENE 1: …

EXT. PLACE - NIGHT #1#
= One sentence on what this scene does.

Establishing action in one or two sentences. NAME (30s), what they look like and wear.

[[Hold: 2.5s.]]

===

NARRATOR (V.O.)
One spoken line.

NAME
(how it is said)
Their line.

CUT TO:

INT. ANOTHER PLACE - CONTINUOUS #2#
= …

…

FADE OUT.
```

## 10. Check before you hand it over

1. Title page has Title, Credit, Author, Source, Draft date, Format, **Setting** and **Premise**.
2. Every `#` act line is there; every scene heading starts INT./EXT. and has a `=` synopsis.
3. Every person is introduced once, in capitals, with age, a sex word or pronoun, clothes and a mark.
4. No capitals line stands above action; no heading lacks INT./EXT. (the import's report, under **Check:**, names each such line by its number and says how to fix it: a capitals line alone or ending in a full stop is read as a speaker, so start it with `!`; a place-and-time line without INT./EXT. is not a scene)
5. Every silent picture that should not be 4 seconds has a `[[Hold:]]`; every sound that matters has a `[[Sound:]]`.
6. A page break `===` sits wherever the picture must change.
7. **Check it** (next section), then run the import as a **preview**: it reports chapters, beats, lines, Characters, scenes, sounds, and what the story still lacks (World, Setting, Premise), before anything is made.

## 11. Editing a Fountain with an AI

Give the AI this page and say: *keep every title-page line, every `#` act line, every `=` synopsis, every scene number, and every paragraph and line you were not asked to change, word for word*. Unchanged paragraphs keep their picture and recording when the revision is checked; reworded ones are flagged. Ask for the whole file back, as plain text, then make a **Revision** in Marvin: *check* it, read the report, *apply* it. For a rewrite where little of the old text is left, set the revision to `replace`.

## 12. Check it before it is read

The import reads a Fountain the way the format says, and a slip in the writing is not an error to it: a speaker in lower case is action, a note left open is ignored, two scenes with one number are one, a transition without its colon is a line of the story. Each reads fine and means something else. **Check the Fountain** finds those before anything is made, each with its line and what to write, and costs nothing: it reads the text only.

- **In the Narrate a story setup:** the step *Check the Fountain*, before the split; its report shows under the button. It writes the report in the story's **Fountain check**. Nothing needs approving. An uploaded file can be read on *Story details* (*Read the file*, under the file, with the report's line numbers; the address `#L17` opens it at line 17) but not edited in Marvin: fix it where it came from, then choose or upload it again under *Fountain file* and check again.
- **From the command line, no Marvin needed:** `python -m storyrender check file.fountain` (or `-` for standard input; `--json` for data). It prints what it found, its first line saying whether the import would stop or go ahead, and exits 1 when the import would stop. In the worker image: `docker run --rm -i screenplay-studio-worker python -m storyrender check - < file.fountain`.
- **Through Marvin** (the Marvin CLI, the web app, or an AI over MCP): run the workflow *Screenplay: check some Fountain text* with the text, or *Screenplay: check the Fountain* on a story; both make a `job` of kind `check-fountain` (also queued directly: `args.text`, `args.asset`, or `args.story`). The job's `result` holds `errors`, `looks`, `import_stops`, `report` and `findings`. **An AI writing a Fountain should check it this way before handing it over, fix every error, and check again until there are none.**
- **The import itself** stops on the serious ones (a speaker in lower case that is also written in capitals elsewhere, a note or a bracket left open, a scene number used for two places, a transition with no colon, a Hold or Sound time that is not a number, a section with no title, a heading with no place) and lists them. A preview (dry run) and a revision check only report. To go on anyway, run the import with `accept_errors: yes`. The capitals warnings (a lone line in capitals, a heading with no INT./EXT.) were warnings before and still are: the report lists them, every one, under *Worth a look*.
- **Worth a look, not mistakes:** no title page, no Setting or Premise, a one-word lower-case line above a sentence (a speaker?), a speaker spelled almost like another, characters you cannot see that change how a line reads (a direction mark or a control character; a non-breaking or zero-width space is read as the space it looks like), a stray `===` or `]]`, `>centered<` text (alone it is a plain card, which may be what you want; inside a paragraph it is action).
